learningObjective: Explain the meet operator and lattice ordering choice for a canonical data-flow analysis.
stem: In classical data-flow analysis, the meet operator combines information at a join point (multiple predecessor paths). Which pairing of analysis and meet operator is correct?

options.text: Both liveness and available expressions use union; the direction (forward/backward) is what distinguishes them.
Liveness uses intersection because a variable must be live on all paths to be considered live; available expressions use union to be sound.

Liveness (may-analysis, backward): meet = union — a variable is live-in at a block if it is live-in on some successor. Available expressions (must-analysis, forward): meet = intersection — an expression is available at a block only if it is available on every predecessor path.
Neither analysis uses a meet operator; both are point-to-point dataflow computations without merging.

explanation: Standard textbook pairing: liveness (may-analysis, backward, union) — some path uses the variable in the future. Available expressions (must-analysis, forward, intersection) — every path has computed the expression. The direction (forward/backward) and the may/must nature (union/intersection) are independent and combine into the four-quadrant classification of classical dataflow analyses.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: available expressions use intersection, not union.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: reverses the operators for both analyses.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: liveness = may/backward/union; available expressions = must/forward/intersection.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: both use meet operators at join points.

assumptions: Standard textbook dataflow framework (Dragon Book, EAC3).
nonImplications: Does not imply all meet operators are union or intersection; more elaborate lattices (constant propagation, range analysis) have richer meets.
Does not imply meet direction of forward/backward is arbitrary; each analysis has a natural direction driven by its semantics.
